name: LOGEST

args.name: known_y's
args.about: the values that grow

args.name: known_x's
args.about: the steps they belong to, like 1, 2, 3 (1, 2, 3… if left out)

args.name: const
args.about: FALSE to make the curve start at 1

args.name: stats
args.about: TRUE for extra figures about the fit

about: Finds the growth rate of numbers that grow by a steady percentage, giving the rate and the starting value.

example.why: Users go up about 50% a month, so each month is about 1.5 times the last; the starting value spills into the next cell.

notes: Gives two cells side by side: the growth factor, then the value at step 0. GROWTH uses the same curve to predict new values.

name: LOGNORM.DIST

args.name: x
args.about: the value to look at

args.name: mean
args.about: the mean of the logarithm of the values

args.name: standard_dev
args.about: the spread of the logarithm of the values

args.name: cumulative
args.about: TRUE for the chance of being at or below x, FALSE for the curve's height

about: Gives the chance for a value whose logarithm follows a bell curve, as for incomes or house prices that are mostly small with a long tail of large ones.

example.why: LN(300000) is about 12.61, 0.28 log spreads above the log mean of 12.5, so about 61% of prices are at or below it.

name: LOGNORM.INV

args.name: probability
args.about: the chance, between 0 and 1

args.name: mean
args.about: the mean of the logarithm of the values

args.name: standard_dev
args.about: the spread of the logarithm of the values

about: Works backwards from LOGNORM.DIST: gives the value that a chosen share of a long-tailed set of values falls below.

example.why: 9 in 10 prices are below this: EXP(12.5 + 1.2816 × 0.4).

name: MAXA

args.name: value1
args.about: a value, a cell or a range

args.name: value2
args.about: more values, cells or ranges

about: Gives the largest value, counting TRUE as 1, FALSE and text in cells as 0.

example.why: FALSE counts as 0, which is bigger than -2 and -5.

notes: MAX leaves out TRUE, FALSE and text in cells.

name: MEDIAN

args.name: number1
args.about: a number, a cell or a range

args.name: number2
args.about: more numbers, cells or ranges

about: Gives the middle value when the numbers are put in order.

example.why: In order: 180000, 210000, 250000, 900000; with an even count it takes the halfway point of the two middle ones. The one mansion barely moves it.

name: MINA

args.name: value1
args.about: a value, a cell or a range

args.name: value2
args.about: more values, cells or ranges

about: Gives the smallest value, counting TRUE as 1, FALSE and text in cells as 0.

example.why: TRUE counts as 1, which is smaller than 4 and 7.

notes: MIN leaves out TRUE, FALSE and text in cells.

name: MODE.MULT

args.name: number1
args.about: a number, a cell or a range

args.name: number2
args.about: more numbers, cells or ranges

about: Gives every value that turns up most often, when there's a tie.

example.why: Sizes 6 and 9 each turn up twice; 6 comes first and 9 spills into the cell below.

name: MODE.SNGL

args.name: number1
args.about: a number, a cell or a range

args.name: number2
args.about: more numbers, cells or ranges

about: Gives the value that turns up most often.

example.why: Size 9 turns up twice, every other size once.

notes: Gives #N/A when no value turns up more than once. MODE.MULT gives all the values in a tie.

name: NEGBINOM.DIST

args.name: number_f
args.about: how many failures before the last success

args.name: number_s
args.about: how many successes you want

args.name: probability_s
args.about: the chance of success each try

args.name: cumulative
args.about: TRUE for that many failures or fewer, FALSE for exactly that many

about: Gives the chance of having a set number of failures before reaching a set number of successes.

example.why: The chance that a seller with a 1-in-5 hit rate makes exactly 5 calls that fail before the second sale.

name: NORM.DIST

args.name: x
args.about: the value to look at

args.name: mean
args.about: the average

args.name: standard_dev
args.about: the spread

args.name: cumulative
args.about: TRUE for the chance of being at or below x, FALSE for the curve's height

about: Gives the chance of a value on a bell curve with the average and spread you give.

example.why: 180 cm is 1.25 spreads above the average, and about 89% of people are that tall or shorter.

name: NORM.INV

args.name: probability
args.about: the chance, between 0 and 1

args.name: mean
args.about: the average

args.name: standard_dev
args.about: the spread

about: Works backwards from NORM.DIST: gives the value that a chosen share of a bell curve falls below.

example.why: 95% of people are shorter than this: 170 + 1.645 × 8.

name: NORM.S.DIST

args.name: z
args.about: how many spreads above (or below) the average

args.name: cumulative
args.about: TRUE for the chance of being at or below z, FALSE for the curve's height

about: Gives the chance on the standard bell curve, the one with average 0 and spread 1.

example.why: About 84% of values on a bell curve are less than one spread above the average.

name: NORM.S.INV

args.name: probability
args.about: the chance, between 0 and 1

about: Works backwards from NORM.S.DIST: gives how many spreads from the average a chosen share falls below.

example.why: 97.5% of a bell curve lies below 1.96 spreads above the average; that's where 95% confidence limits come from.

name: PEARSON

args.name: array1
args.about: the first set of values

args.name: array2
args.about: the second set, the same size

about: Measures how closely two sets of numbers rise and fall together, from -1 to 1.

example.why: Near 1: months with more ads had more sales, almost in a straight line.

notes: The same as CORREL.

name: PERCENTILE.EXC

args.name: array
args.about: the values

args.name: k
args.about: the share, between 0 and 1 but not 0 or 1

about: Gives the value that a chosen share of the numbers falls below, leaving out the ends.

example.why: A quarter of the way up the scores 62, 68, 74, 75, 81, 90, counted over 7 gaps rather than 5.

notes: PERCENTILE.INC counts from the lowest to the highest value; the two give slightly different answers.

name: PERCENTILE.INC

args.name: array
args.about: the values

args.name: k
args.about: the share, from 0 to 1

about: Gives the value that a chosen share of the numbers falls below.

example.why: 9 in 10 of the scores are at or below this: 90% of the way from 62 to 90 in order, between 81 and 90.

name: PERCENTRANK.EXC

args.name: array
args.about: the values

args.name: x
args.about: the value to rank

args.name: significance
args.about: how many digits to keep (3 if left out)

about: Gives where a value stands among the numbers as a share between 0 and 1, never exactly 0 or 1.

example.why: 75 is 4th of 6 in order, so it is 4 ÷ 7 of the way up.

name: PERCENTRANK.INC

args.name: array
args.about: the values

args.name: x
args.about: the value to rank

args.name: significance
args.about: how many digits to keep (3 if left out)

about: Gives where a value stands among the numbers as a share from 0 (lowest) to 1 (highest).

example.why: Three of the other five scores are below 75: 3 ÷ 5.

name: PERMUT

args.name: number
args.about: how many to choose from

args.name: number_chosen
args.about: how many to pick

about: Counts the ways to pick some items when the order matters and nothing can be picked twice.

example.why: Gold, silver and bronze among 8 runners: 8 × 7 × 6.

name: PERMUTATIONA

args.name: number
args.about: how many to choose from

args.name: number_chosen
args.about: how many to pick

about: Counts the ways to pick some items when the order matters and the same one can be picked again.

example.why: A bike lock with 4 wheels of 10 digits: 10 × 10 × 10 × 10.

name: PHI

args.name: x
args.about: how many spreads from the average

about: Gives the height of the standard bell curve at a point.

example.why: The bell curve is highest at the middle, where its height is 1 ÷ √(2π).

notes: The same as NORM.S.DIST(x,FALSE).

name: POISSON.DIST

args.name: x
args.about: how many times it happens

args.name: mean
args.about: how many times it happens on average

args.name: cumulative
args.about: TRUE for that many or fewer, FALSE for exactly that many

about: Gives the chance of something happening a set number of times, when you know how often it happens on average.

example.why: With 5 customers an hour on average, exactly 3 in an hour happens about 14% of the time.

name: PROB

args.name: x_range
args.about: the possible values

args.name: prob_range
args.about: the chance of each, adding up to 1

args.name: lower_limit
args.about: the lowest value to count

args.name: upper_limit
args.about: the highest value to count (just the lower one if left out)

about: Adds up the chances of the values that fall between two limits.

example.why: 1 goal or 2 goals: 0.35 + 0.25.

name: QUARTILE.EXC

args.name: array
args.about: the values

args.name: quart
args.about: 1 for the lower quarter, 2 for the middle, 3 for the upper quarter

about: Gives the value a quarter, half or three quarters of the way up the numbers, leaving out the ends.

example.why: Three quarters of the way up 62, 68, 74, 75, 81, 90, counted over 7 gaps.

notes: Same as PERCENTILE.EXC with 0.25, 0.5 or 0.75. QUARTILE.INC gives slightly different answers.

name: QUARTILE.INC

args.name: array
args.about: the values

args.name: quart
args.about: 0 for the lowest, 1 for the lower quarter, 2 for the middle, 3 for the upper quarter, 4 for the highest

about: Gives the value a quarter, half or three quarters of the way up the numbers.

example.why: A quarter of the way from the lowest to the highest score, between 68 and 74.

name: RANK.AVG

args.name: number
args.about: the value to rank

args.name: ref
args.about: the values to rank it among

args.name: order
args.about: 0 or left out to put the largest first, 1 for the smallest first

about: Gives a value's place among the numbers; tied values share the average of their places.

example.why: Bob and Cara tie for 2nd and 3rd place, so each gets 2.5.

name: RANK.EQ

args.name: number
args.about: the value to rank

args.name: ref
args.about: the values to rank it among

args.name: order
args.about: 0 or left out to put the largest first, 1 for the smallest first

about: Gives a value's place among the numbers; tied values share the best place.

example.why: Bob and Cara tie, so both are 2nd and Dev is 4th.

notes: RANK.AVG gives ties the average of their places.

name: SKEW

args.name: number1
args.about: a number, a cell or a range

args.name: number2
args.about: more numbers, cells or ranges

about: Measures how lopsided the numbers are: above 0 means a long tail of high values, below 0 a long tail of low ones.

example.why: Most waits are short but one is 15 minutes, so the tail points to the high side.

notes: Treats the numbers as a sample; SKEW.P treats them as everything there is.

name: SKEW.P

args.name: number1
args.about: a number, a cell or a range

args.name: number2
args.about: more numbers, cells or ranges

about: Measures how lopsided the numbers are, treating them as everything there is rather than a sample.

example.why: The same long tail of high waits; a little smaller than SKEW because it doesn't allow for sampling.

name: SMALL

args.name: array
args.about: the values

args.name: k
args.about: 1 for the smallest, 2 for the next…

about: Gives the smallest value, the second smallest and so on.

example.why: In order: 61.9, 62.8, 63.5, 64.2; the second is 62.8.

notes: LARGE counts from the top.

name: STANDARDIZE

args.name: x
args.about: the value

args.name: mean
args.about: the average

args.name: standard_dev
args.about: the spread

about: Says how many spreads a value is above or below the average (its z-score).

example.why: (82 − 70) ÷ 8: the score is one and a half spreads above average.

name: STDEV

args.name: number1
args.about: a number, a cell or a range

args.name: number2
args.about: more numbers, cells or ranges

about: Measures how spread out a sample of numbers is around their average.

example.why: The scores are typically about 10 points from their average of 75.

notes: An older name for STDEV.S, kept for old spreadsheets.

name: STDEV.P

args.name: number1
args.about: a number, a cell or a range

args.name: number2
args.about: more numbers, cells or ranges

about: Measures how spread out the numbers are around their average, when they are everything there is (not a sample).

example.why: The square root of the average squared distance from 75; a bit smaller than STDEV.S.

notes: Use STDEV.S when the numbers are a sample of a bigger group.

name: STDEV.S

args.name: number1
args.about: a number, a cell or a range

args.name: number2
args.about: more numbers, cells or ranges

about: Measures how spread out a sample of numbers is around their average.

example.why: The scores are typically about 10 points from their average of 75; it divides by 5 rather than 6 to allow for this being a sample.

notes: STDEV.P is for when the numbers are everything there is.

name: STDEVA

args.name: value1
args.about: a value, a cell or a range

args.name: value2
args.about: more values, cells or ranges

about: Measures how spread out a sample is, counting TRUE as 1, FALSE and text in cells as 0.

example.why: The values are taken as 4, 1, 6 and 0.

notes: STDEV.S leaves out TRUE, FALSE and text in cells.

name: STDEVPA

args.name: value1
args.about: a value, a cell or a range

args.name: value2
args.about: more values, cells or ranges

about: Measures how spread out all the values are, counting TRUE as 1, FALSE and text in cells as 0.

example.why: The values are taken as 4, 1, 6 and 0, treated as everything there is.

notes: STDEV.P leaves out TRUE, FALSE and text in cells.

name: T.DIST

args.name: x
args.about: the t value

args.name: deg_freedom
args.about: the degrees of freedom, usually the sample size minus 1

args.name: cumulative
args.about: TRUE for the chance of being at or below x, FALSE for the curve's height

about: Gives the chance on the t curve, a wider bell curve used for small samples.

example.why: About 96.3% of the t curve for a sample of 11 lies below 2.

name: T.DIST.2T

args.name: x
args.about: the t value (0 or more)

args.name: deg_freedom
args.about: the degrees of freedom, usually the sample size minus 1

about: Gives the chance of a t value at least this far from 0 in either direction.

example.why: About 3.7% above 2 plus the same below −2.

name: T.DIST.RT

args.name: x
args.about: the t value

args.name: deg_freedom
args.about: the degrees of freedom, usually the sample size minus 1

about: Gives the chance of a t value above x.

example.why: The part of the t curve above 2: 1 minus T.DIST.

name: T.INV

args.name: probability
args.about: the chance, between 0 and 1

args.name: deg_freedom
args.about: the degrees of freedom, usually the sample size minus 1

about: Works backwards from T.DIST: gives the t value that a chosen share of the t curve falls below.

example.why: 95% of the t curve for 10 degrees of freedom lies below this; wider than the 1.645 of a bell curve.

name: T.INV.2T

args.name: probability
args.about: the chance in both tails together, between 0 and 1

args.name: deg_freedom
args.about: the degrees of freedom, usually the sample size minus 1

about: Gives how far from 0 a t value has to be so that only the chosen chance lies further out, on both sides together.

example.why: Only 5% of the t curve lies beyond ±2.23; this is the number for a 95% confidence interval from a sample of 11.

name: T.TEST

args.name: array1
args.about: the first set of values

args.name: array2
args.about: the second set

args.name: tails
args.about: 1 to test one direction, 2 for either

args.name: type
args.about: 1 for paired values, 2 for two groups with the same spread, 3 for groups with different spreads

about: Gives the chance that the difference between two sets of numbers is just luck.

example.why: Every runner got faster after training; a chance this small says the change is very unlikely to be luck.

name: TREND

args.name: known_y's
args.about: the values you know

args.name: known_x's
args.about: what they belong to, like months (1, 2, 3… if left out)

args.name: new_x's
args.about: where to predict (the known x's if left out)

args.name: const
args.about: FALSE to make the line pass through 0

about: Draws the best straight line through the numbers and gives values along it, to predict new ones.

example.why: The line through the months' ads and sales predicts the sales for a month with 10 ads.

name: TRIMMEAN

args.name: array
args.about: the values

args.name: percent
args.about: the share to leave out, split between the top and bottom

about: Gives the average after leaving out the highest and lowest values.

example.why: 20% of 10 scores is 2, so the lowest (2) and highest (9.9) are left out and the other 8 are averaged.

name: VAR.P

args.name: number1
args.about: a number, a cell or a range

args.name: number2
args.about: more numbers, cells or ranges

about: Measures how spread out the numbers are: the average squared distance from their average, when they are everything there is.

example.why: The scores' distances from 75, squared and averaged over all 6.

notes: VAR.S is for a sample. STDEV.P is its square root, in the same units as the data.

name: VAR.S

args.name: number1
args.about: a number, a cell or a range

args.name: number2
args.about: more numbers, cells or ranges

about: Measures how spread out a sample of numbers is: the squared distance from their average, averaged over one fewer than the count.

example.why: The scores' squared distances from 75 add up to 480, divided by 5.

notes: STDEV.S is its square root, in the same units as the data.

name: VARPA

args.name: value1
args.about: a value, a cell or a range

args.name: value2
args.about: more values, cells or ranges

about: Measures how spread out all the values are, counting TRUE as 1, FALSE and text in cells as 0.

example.why: The values are taken as 4, 1, 6 and 0; their average is 2.75.

notes: VAR.P leaves out TRUE, FALSE and text in cells.

name: VARA

args.name: value1
args.about: a value, a cell or a range

args.name: value2
args.about: more values, cells or ranges

about: Measures how spread out a sample is, counting TRUE as 1, FALSE and text in cells as 0.

example.why: The values are taken as 4, 1, 6 and 0, divided by 3 rather than 4 as for a sample.

notes: VAR.S leaves out TRUE, FALSE and text in cells.

name: WEIBULL.DIST

args.name: x
args.about: the value, like a time

args.name: alpha
args.about: the shape: below 1 for early failures, above 1 for wearing out

args.name: beta
args.about: the scale, roughly the typical value

args.name: cumulative
args.about: TRUE for the chance of being at or below x, FALSE for the curve's height

about: Gives the chance used for how long things last, like the chance a part has failed by a certain time.

example.why: 1 − EXP(−(1000 ÷ 2000)²): about 22% of the bulbs have failed by 1000 hours.

name: Z.TEST

args.name: array
args.about: the sample

args.name: x
args.about: the average to test against

args.name: sigma
args.about: the known spread (the sample's own if left out)

about: Gives the chance of a sample average this high or higher if the true average were x.

example.why: The bags average 503 g; if the machine really filled 500 g with a spread of 3 g, an average this high would happen about 1.3% of the time.

name: CORREL

args.name: array1
args.about: the first set of values

args.name: array2
args.about: the second set, the same size

about: Measures how closely two sets of numbers rise and fall together, from -1 to 1.

example.why: Near 1: months with more ads had more sales, almost in a straight line.

notes: The same as PEARSON. RSQ is its square.

name: RSQ

args.name: known_y's
args.about: the values to explain

args.name: known_x's
args.about: the values that explain them

about: Says how much of the ups and downs in one set of numbers a straight line through another explains, from 0 to 1.

example.why: The square of CORREL: the number of ads explains almost all the change in sales.

name: INTERCEPT

args.name: known_y's
args.about: the values to predict

args.name: known_x's
args.about: the values to predict them from

about: Gives where the best straight line through the numbers crosses 0: the predicted value when x is 0.

example.why: The line through ads and sales predicts these sales in a month with no ads.

notes: SLOPE gives how steep the line is.

name: SLOPE

args.name: known_y's
args.about: the values to predict

args.name: known_x's
args.about: the values to predict them from

about: Gives how steep the best straight line through the numbers is: how much y goes up for each 1 that x goes up.

example.why: Each extra ad goes with about 7.6 more sales.

notes: INTERCEPT gives where the line crosses 0.

name: STEYX

args.name: known_y's
args.about: the values to predict

args.name: known_x's
args.about: the values to predict them from

about: Gives how far, typically, the values are from the best straight line through them.

example.why: Predicting sales from the line through ads and sales is typically off by this many sales.
